The 10213 meeting of the Security Council is called to order. The provisional agenda for this meeting is maintenance of international peace and security, food on the fire, the Security Council's role in mitigating global and local food crisis. And the agenda is adopted. Before each of you is a list of speakers who have requested to participate. in accordance with Rule 37 and 39 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, we propose that they be invited to participate in this meeting. There being no objection, it is so decided. The Security Council will now begin its consideration of item two of the agenda. I wish to draw the attention of Council members to document S/2026/650, letter dated 4 August 2026 from the Permanent Representative of Denmark to the United Nations addressed to the Secretary-General transmitting a concept paper on the item under consideration. And I warmly welcome the Secretary-General, His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, and I will give him the floor, please.

Mr. President, Excellencies, I thank the Government of Denmark and Minister Rasmussen for chairing this urgent discussion on conflict and food security. This is an opportunity for the Council to address a dangerous and evolving reality. Critical food systems and the lives and livelihoods they sustain are under attack. Getting enough to eat is a basic human need, a need that is clearly reflected in Sustainable Development Goal 2 ending hunger. Zero hunger is achievable, but it requires tackling hunger's many root causes, including conflict. In resolution 2417, this Council highlighted the link between conflict induced food insecurity and the threat of famine and armed conflict and violence. and it provided clear guidance to ensure the proper functioning of food systems and markets in the midst of conflict. Today is about strengthening the implementation of that important resolution, and there is no time to lose. Across the Sahel, farmers are driven from their fields as conflict disrupts farming, trade and livelihoods, and food insecurity worsens across the region. In Sudan, Markets have been hit by drone strikes and missiles. In Haiti, gang violence has cut off entire communities. And humanitarian workers have been denied access to assist people in desperate need, from Gaza to Mali, Myanmar and Sudan. Some have come under direct attack and even killed. It is no coincidence that 2025 saw not only the highest number of armed conflicts since World War II, but also among the highest levels of global acute hunger on record, with at least 266 million people facing acute food insecurity. 2025 also marked the first time this century that two famines were confirmed simultaneously in Sudan and Gaza. A shameful milestone. The UN's latest Hunger Hotspot report shows that conflict and violence are the primary drivers in 12 out of 13 hunger hotspots of greatest concern. The link between armed conflict, violence and hunger is undeniable. We know that rising hunger can fuel displacement, fragility, instability and competition for scarce resources. The effects are borderless, with conflicts and violence triggering shockwaves of hunger across borders and regions. The war in Ukraine is affecting grain and energy exports in the Black Sea, both from Ukraine and Russia. The crisis in the Middle East is another example. The Strait of Hormuz carries about a fifth of global oil supplies and a third of global fertiliser trade. Restrictions and closures have driven up commodity prices and made availability plummet. And attacks on commercial vessels in the Red Sea are further threatening supply chains for food and other commodities. For import dependent countries, many struggling with high debt, this directly increases the cost of farming and imperils future harvests. We need a peaceful, just and durable settlement that safeguards international navigational rights and freedoms, including in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el Mandeb Strait, and restore stability and confidence. As I detailed yesterday, we have worked to develop and propose practical mechanisms to address global humanitarian needs triggered by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. This time bound confidence building effort would focus initially on fertilisers and related raw materials, but with the ability to be extended to other products. International support for this initiative has been encouraging. But what is needed now is the cooperation and political will of the parties, and I urge all concerned to engage seriously and constructively. But this effort cannot be seen as a substitute for fully restoring navigational rights and freedoms in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Excellencies, resolution 2417 recognises the need to break the vicious cycle between armed conflict and food insecurity. Yet the vicious cycle rolls on. So today I call on this Council to consider three measures to strengthen and build on this landmark resolution. First, resolution 2417 must be implemented consistently and in full. For parties to conflict, this means not depriving civilians of objects indispensable to their survival, including food, crops, livestock and drinking water supplies, and refraining from attacking, destroying, removing or rendering them useless. It also means taking constant care to spare civilian objects necessary for food production and distribution, including farms, mills, water systems, food processing and storage sites and transportation hubs. It means providing humanitarian personnel with safe and unimpeded access to civilians in armed conflicts. Too many parties to armed conflict, disregard their obligations under international humanitarian law with impunity, and this is unacceptable. States must do their part to uphold and ensure respect for international humanitarian law and use their influence to secure compliance. Throughout, reporting on conflict-induced hunger New famine risks and emerging risks to food systems and humanitarian operations must be acted upon. We cannot wait for famine or catastrophic conditions to be formally confirmed. I call on this Council to act when the warning lights are flashing. Second, food systems must be protected in their entirety. Conflicts or violence must not keep farmers from their fields, keep crops trapped in or on the ground, or keep food supplies stuck in storage. I call on this Council to renew its support for protections for infrastructure essential to food security. That must include safeguards for farms, water systems, markets, storage facilities, ports and supply routes. It should also reinforce safeguards for the supply of food exports, agricultural inputs and humanitarian aid, including passage across borders and seas.

Your Excellencies, the third, humanitarians must be protected. All parties to conflict have clear obligations under international humanitarian law. That includes allowing practical arrangements that enable humanitarian operations and protecting humanitarian workers as they carry out their life-saving work. In resolution 2417, this Council expressed its willingness to consider information on the unlawful denial of humanitarian access and take appropriate steps, including sanction measures. I call on this Council to make every effort to ensure accountability, to keep vital humanitarian aid flowing, and to protect those delivering it. Your Excellencies, the best protection against food insecurity is peace, and the safest conditions for peace are a world without hunger. I urge this Council to use all tools at its disposal to help prevent and end conflicts and to stop emerging risks from becoming wider crises of instability and, in particular, of food insecurity. I thank you.
I thank the Secretary-General for his briefing. Now I will give the floor to Mr. Kael Skau.

Thank you, Mr. President, and thanks to the government of Denmark, to you, Minister Rasmussen, for convening us on this timely and important topic. And let me also recognize and thank the Secretary General for his leadership. It was your letter, Mr. Secretary General, that triggered the discussion back in '17 that led to this important resolution, the resolution 2417, a year later. Indeed, a landmark resolution adopted by consensus recognizing the vicious conflict hunger cycle, how conflict drives hunger, but also how hunger fuels conflict. Excellencies, I was one of you back then representing a member state on this council. Today, I'm proud to represent the World Food Programme, an organization awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020 for its efforts to combat hunger, but also for its contribution to bettering conditions for peace in conflict areas. That was a time of optimism for the World Food Programme. With strong support of this Council and with the recognition of the Nobel Committee, we thought a world without hunger was within reach. But fast forward to today, 2026, only six years later, and the picture is very different. The vicious conflict hunger cycle is instead accelerating. In this short period of time, the number of acutely food insecure has increased threefold, while funding for operations has plummeted. And as Deschi just pointed out, it's more dangerous than ever for our colleagues in the field. In my role at WFP, I have the privilege to frequently visit frontline teams in the most complex of environments. Today, I will draw from that firsthand experience, sharing with you what the conflict hunger cycle really looks like in practice, and of course, point to how the Security Council, in our view, can and should respond. Excellencies, I spent last week in Somalia. literally speaking to you with the dust of Burhakaba still on my shoes. I saw camps full of families who had their lives and their homes and their lands taken away when non-state armed groups arrived. One family with four children that I sat down to speak with had left a multi-generation farm where they had farmed, fed themselves, and made an income. Armed groups had rolled in, demanding taxes to keep farming. So they had decided it was safer to flee to displacement camp some hundred kilometers by foot. They had lost everything, including one child on that journey. The other three kids were now growing up in a camp and without a school to go to. These sudden insurgencies keep erupting across Somalia. Like in Baidoa last week, fighting prevented my planned visit there. But much worse, it prevented our operations. Some 5,000 kids did not get WFP nutritious food in Baidoa that day. In addition to insecurity, hunger in Somalia is also driven by two consecutive droughts, and the super El Nino is expected to bring heavy flooding in November. This all adds to a catastrophic malnutrition and food crisis. Nearly two million children suffering from acute and severe malnutrition, A third of the population, six million people, face acute hunger or worse. And Somalis are facing this perfect storm at the very moment that global engagement is at its lowest. As you well know, the UNSAS mandate beyond the end of 26 is uncertain. And support from humanitarian action is shrinking. One key donor no longer provides any funding, and no others are stepping in. In 2022, facing a similar situation, WFP and partners prevented famine. Thanks to generous donor support, not least from the US, we scaled up assistance to nearly 10 million people. Today, WFP is only assisting some 600,000, one in 10 in acute need, and millions are left out. Many could die. Famine is getting closer. This should be a wake-up call for everyone. It's not only an issue for Somalia, because when families can't put food on their table, they are left with three choices, starve, move, or rebel. These are perfect conditions for armed groups, criminal gangs, exploitative businesses to recruit vulnerable young people. So in Somalia, but also in places like Guatemala and the DRC over the past few weeks, I've spoken to parents terrified that their children will soon be in military camps, street corners, or mines instead of in schools. Excellencies, beyond this vicious cycle that we have been warning you for years now, there is a new dimension that needs your attention and your action. Consequences of conflict is now also being transmitted thousands of miles through interconnected economies and trading systems across borders and seas. Some have spoken about a double choke point crisis, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. But yesterday, the Secretary General rightly came with warnings about a triple choke point crisis, adding the recent escalation in the Black Sea. These serious disruptions to maritime trade now threatens to push tens of millions more people into food insecurity. Starting with the conflict in the Gulf, an oil tanker anchored in the Strait of Hormuz can mean one less meal a day for a child in Sudan, where basic food costs are up almost 40% since February this year. And food systems rely on fuel, irrigation, transport, milling. So when oil prices go up, so does the price of flour, rice, and vegetables. And suffocation of fertilizer exports has also hit this planting season hard across Africa and Asia. We are deeply worried about the lag effects this will have on upcoming harvests. At WFP, we have also been exposed to 20% higher shipping costs, 35% more on fuel for our airdrops and our humanitarian flights, meaning less assistance for the people we serve. Second, the de facto Houthi authority strikes on commercial vessels in the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait. This has led to further reduction of trade in the Red Sea and is compromising another export route, regional transit to the Suez Canal. It means further rising prices for people across the globe, but it's also hitting Yemen itself particularly hard, a country that imports 90% of its food. And third, escalating Russian and Ukrainian tax in the Black Sea. Russia and Ukraine exports equal one third of global wheat supply. Grain shipments through the Bosphorus Strait are now down 40% year on year. Import dependent countries like Somalia, who buys 90% of its cereal, are highly exposed. Also, there are longer term risks if the Black Sea ports and shipping lanes stay shut. Farmers will simply have less income and incentives to plant crops for 2027. The world simply cannot afford these layers of crisis. How many choking points before we are completely suffocated? Excellencies, there is just no time to lose. Building on the Secretary-General's call today, WFP looks to the Security Council for urgent and concrete action. just like the response you took to the SG's letter back in 2017. To break the conflict hunger cycle and building on the SG's call, I'm coming to you with five circuit breakers. First, instigate measures to stop conflict in one region, creating hunger in another. Initiatives that ensure free flow of humanitarian aid, Commercial food exports, agricultural inputs via maritime or land corridors are urgently needed. Second, use resolution 2417 much earlier. Act on warning signs. Take action before famine is declared and before agricultural seasons are lost. Just look at Sudan. With decisive early action, we may have prevented famine last year in the world's worst hunger crisis. We all saw the atrocities in Al-Fashir coming, but the international community, including this Council, failed to act on those warnings. It's hard to do justice to the scale of suffering in Sudan, but it really hit me in April when I visited the Tawila camp in Darfur, where survivors of Al-Fashir have gathered. I have never seen anything like it, 700,000 people in a super city of grass huts. They arrived from Al-Fashir with absolutely nothing, traumatized, and they now depend on a trickle of aid to survive. The people I met there felt completely abandoned. I can't say this strong enough, waiting for famine to be declared is a total failure of duty. In the last Somalia famine in 2010 to '12, nearly 260,000 people died, half of them children. We avoided this in 2017 and in 2022 because we acted early on warnings and scaled up assistance. Third, stronger protection for civilians, civilian infrastructure and food systems. The principles of distinction and proportionality must be respected. I was in Lebanon in March, just a few days after the war started. meeting people whose lives had again been snatched away by strikes and evacuation orders. Overnight, they went from daily commute to a life in shelter. Like the family I met in a dingy abandoned hotel in Beirut, in the south of Beirut. As missiles ran down, their world had shrunk to the size of that small hotel room. They told me that the only time they went outside was to collect the daily WFP hot meals. Fourth, protect humanitarian personnel. In northern Yemen, there is a growing acute hunger, but the UN is unable to intervene at this moment of extreme fragility. We have been forced to pause humanitarian work because the operating environment is simply non-existent with the targeting of our staff. Currently, 73 UN staff, including 38 from WFP, are detained by the de facto Houthi authorities. Not a day goes by without thinking of them and of their families. Fifth and finally, more solidarity with the world's most vulnerable. For every story I've told you here today, there are millions untold. I'm thinking about the women and girls I met in Afghanistan back in May. I will never forget my visit to a rural clinic outside Jalalabad. exhausted cries of babies, the panic in the voices of their mothers. Some had walked for hours with skeletal babies in their arms. But at this clinic, normally supported by WFP and UNICEF, we had nothing to give them. Afghanistan is today the world's worst malnutrition crisis, but there is an appalling lack of funds. We are currently turning away six in seven malnourished women and children. WFP hotlines are flooded with calls from parents considering suicide as their children waste away. I used to talk about taking from the hungry to feed the starving. But in the very worst hunger crisis, we are now on the verge of having nothing to give at all. We all risk becoming bystanders as parents, children, and babies starve. Excellencies, let me reassure you that at WFP and with our partners, we are doing everything possible to adapt to a new funding landscape. We are seizing the Secretary-General's UN and 80 reform agenda and the humanitarian reset in full and with ambition. We are doing our absolute best to do better with less. But we need Member States to step up too, to correct course, fund humanitarian action, seek political solutions to conflicts, and reverse the normalization of hunger. We know this is possible. A year ago, I visited Gaza around the time that famine was declared. It was like a dystopian film set. Everywhere we drove, obliterated rubble, every street filled with desperate children looking for food. I returned in January this year after the October ceasefire and adoption of resolution 2803 in November. Still far from a rosy picture, that's for sure. But the ceasefire had improved somewhat food security and reversed famine. And some people that I met had even started to have hope again. I spent time with one displaced family who had returned to the destroyed house in the southern parts of Gaza City. and they were busy trying to recultivate a vineyard amid the rubble to rebuild a family livelihood and tradition. I spoke with bright teenage girls getting WFP food in a UNICEF round school makeshift or makeshift school. They told me they hope to grow up as doctors, pilots and business owners. So as the SG said, these are fragile gains, only a glimmer of hope. Recovery and reconstruction are still far, far away, but it shows what is possible if there is political will. Excellencies, we simply can't fail the people of Gaza again just when conditions are starting to improve. We can't pull back in Sudan just as we secure access for scaling up. And we can't disengage in Somalia and wait for famine to unfold. This Council has shown before that it can be part of breaking the vicious cycle of hunger and conflict. Let today's meeting be the starting point for new bold action to give hundreds of millions of people a path away from hunger and violence back to peace and stability. I thank you.
I thank Mr. Skaal for his briefing and I will give the floor to Dr. Perrine Benoit.

Excellencies, distinguished members of this council, my name is Perrine Benoit and I am the co-CEO of Action Against Hunger. I speak to you today on behalf of the Coalition Against Conflict and Hunger, a group of global organizations working to prevent and limit the impact of conflict on food security and nutrition and to protect civilians from conflict-induced hunger. Resolution 2417 was unanimously adopted by this council in 2018. It was supposed to avert famine and it was supposed to end the vicious circle between conflict and hunger. Yet time and again, its provision have been violated by parties to conflict while implementation by the members of this council have fallen far short from what the resolution demands. Since the resolution was passed, the IPC confirmed famine in parts of South Sudan, Sudan and the Gaza Strip. We have recorded more than 9,300 incidents in over 45 countries in which conflict-related violence impacted civilian infrastructures vital to food systems, including more than 3,200 bombings of markets, agricultural lands, and water systems. And this is just the tip of the iceberg. In Sudan, over 900 attacks on food systems have been recorded since April 2023. including livestock looting, attacks on markets, and violence against people accessing said markets. Famine has been confirmed in multiple areas of the country, while alert persists in many parts. Yet we have failed to see urgent action to bring about a meaningful resolution to the conflict. At the same time, new conflict have led to global macroeconomic shocks, disrupting supply chains and critical infrastructures, driving up food and fuel prices, and increasing the cost of key agricultural inputs and humanitarian aid, threatening efforts to realize the right to food everywhere. This global disruption have a spiraling effect. The conflict in the Gulf has impacted the agricultural production of over 80% of households. Higher fuel costs, constrained agricultural inputs, fertilizer shortages are now the new normal, and we know that vulnerabilities compound. In Sudan, simply being a woman today has become a statistically significant predictor of starvation. This is a vicious circle that we must break. Conflict drives hunger, while hunger and the destruction of livelihoods, in turn, deeply undermine the protection of civilians, drive displacement, and fuel instability. Sudan is now the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis, as my colleague was saying. And it's a stark reminder that hunger is not simply a consequence of conflict, but part of its dynamics. Humanitarian organizations have also had to cope with global disruptions and witness their daily impacts. I like to talk about Yemen, where more than half of the children under five, about 2.2 million, are expected to be acutely malnourished in 2026, alongside 1.3 million pregnant or breastfeeding women. Ahmed is a four-year-old from a remote village, and a few months ago, he was diagnosed with critical severe acute malnutrition. His mother feared for his life, but thanks to lifesaving therapeutic nutrition programs and treatments, he recovered and is healthy today. But for years, procuring the supplies needed to treat acute malnutrition in Yemen has already been an incredible challenge. It has now become even more difficult. The cost of sea transport for humanitarian organizations has risen by over 300%. And even more concerning, shipments face major delays. We have to understand that the timeline for a child experiencing malnutrition is brutally short. Within two weeks of losing access to sufficient food, clinical signs of acute malnutrition begin to appear. Within three weeks, children become susceptible to common illnesses that can now kill them. They experience severe wasting, struggle to move, and their organs begin to shut down. Without treatment, the risk of death rises significantly. When stocks run out, this will determine our ability to save children like Ahmed. For them, global trends are absolutely not abstract. They determine whether lifesaving treatment reaches them in time or not. As humanitarian actors, we are doing the best we can in our power to respond to support communities. We remain present, operational, and ready to scale up humanitarian responses despite facing increasingly severe constraints. These constraints include restricted access, but also bureaucratic hurdles, criminalization, disinformation, and growing threats, direct attacks. More than 1,000 humanitarian workers have been killed in the last three years. And during the same period, we recorded over 700 attacks on humanitarian food aid activities. For decades, the humanitarian system has built the expertise to support local and national food systems and markets. But today, massive funding cuts, shrinking access, global disruptions, and threats to food security surveillance systems are putting the quality and effectiveness of humanitarian responses at increasing risk. The recent decision to end FEWS NET monitoring in Yemen, among other countries, is a clear example of this. As food insecurity rises, tracking systems are being lost. We are at risk of losing our capacity for early warning. We need the access, protection and support necessary to put that expertise into practice and invest in anticipatory actions and local solutions at scale. To do so, the coalition has three main asks to this Council. First, use UNSCR 2417 as an early warning and prevention tool grounded in the perspective of communities affected. We know what happened when food systems are destroyed. The consequences are foreseeable. We have the warning signs, attacks on food systems, logistical and supply chain disruptions, food prices shocks, they all signal emerging risk for food security and peace, and we have the policy frameworks. What is missing is the political will and early action to address the drivers of conflict-induced hunger at both micro and macro scales. To do so, this council must protect civil society voices, particularly those of affected communities. As the distance grows between this hall of power and those most affected by your decisions, the council and UN member states must close that gap, reverse shrinking civil space, and invest in the information systems that underpin early action. When reports on attacks on food systems and emerging food security risks are shared, the Council must promptly and systematically respond to driving investigation, acting on recommendations set out in white notes, and calling for Council-level action. This matters because conflict and hunger reinforce one another in a virtuous circle. Conflict drives hunger, while severe food insecurity, disrupted livelihoods, and rising food prices can deepen tensions, fuel instability, and contribute to conflict dynamics. Ultimately, the Council must move beyond documenting hunger and act on the information on attacks on food systems before today's shocks become tomorrow's famines and security crises. Second, we asked that you take urgent and decisive diplomatic actions to uphold international law. Condemnation ring hollow when they are not matched by action. This Council must ensure that no party to a conflict uses starvation as a weapon of war or acts in ways that exacerbate conflict-induced hunger by either attacking, destroying, removing, or rendering useless objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population. And it must hold perpetrators accountable. The use of siege tactics against civilians is prohibited and must never be accepted. We call on this Council to protect the humanitarian actors and infrastructures, safeguard humanitarian access, thus ensuring safe, rapid, sustained and unimpeded actions throughout affected areas. When food systems are disrupted, people's reliance on humanitarian assistance increases. If access is blocked, hunger deepens. Member States should support access negotiations as well as practical solutions that guarantee safe, rapid and predictable humanitarian access, including in contexts under international or national sanctions, So you make an exemption and diplomacy in line with existing resolutions. Third, we all need to invest in local food systems. Disruption to the global food systems are amplifying the impact of conflict on already fragile food systems. These pressures can deepen tensions, drive displacement, and further compound existing conflict dynamics. We must therefore strive to make food systems more local, sustainable, and resilient, and pivot from a state of perpetual crisis management to one of investment in resilience. That means prioritizing local solutions and investing in local production and resilient supply chain. It also means reinstating quality humanitarian funding, supporting first and foremost local and national NGOs, including women-led organizations. This Council has a responsibility to prevent and manage conflict, to protect civilians, and to support accountability. Breaking the cycle of conflict and hunger requires political action, and political action is a choice, but so is inaction. The world is watching, and it cannot wait any longer. Thank you.

Thank Dr. Benoit for her briefing. And I shall now make a statement in my capacity as the Minister for Foreign Affairs of Denmark. Let me start by thanking you, Secretary-General Guterres, Acting Executive Director Skov and Co-Chief Executive Officer Dr. Benoit for your remarks and importantly your recommendations. Excellencies, eight years ago, this Council adopted a landmark resolution on conflict and hunger that explicitly recognizes the link between armed conflict and hunger and food insecurity. It also condemned the starvation of civilians as a method of warfare. That resolution contained a number, 74 million, the number of people facing conflict-induced hunger around the world at that time. Today, a few years later, that number has doubled to 147 million. Conflict remains the primary driver of hunger, accounting for more than half of all people facing severe hunger. More than 20,000 attacks on markets, farmland and food distribution systems have been recorded since the adoption of 2417 in 2018. Excellencies, food is under fire. Crops are burned, markets attacked, aid denied. In Sudan, the warring parties have targeted agriculture, attacked UN warehouses and denied access to relief while famine was confirmed on their watch. In Gaza, a period of blockading aid and continued restrictions have left children stunted, destroyed farmland, and an entire population dependent on supplies that barely make it through. For the first time this century, in 2025, famine was declared in two different places in the same time, in Sudan and in Gaza. In relation to both crises, members of this Council have recalled that the use of starvation as a weapon of war is clearly banned under international humanitarian law. The UN has in addition warned of the risk of famine in South Sudan and Somalia before the end of this year. So let us be clear. The blocking international creation and use of hunger and starvation of civilians as a method of warfare constitute a brutal and illegal tactic wherever and whenever it is committed. Excellencies, wars are now colliding with the global food system itself and increasing hunger across borders and continents. In the wake of the illegal Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Black Sea crisis taught us what happens when a breadbasket becomes a battlefield. Sadly, the flow of food supplies in the Black Sea is now again disrupted. Iran's unlawful closure of the Strait of Hormuz is just another example of what happens when a vital passageway for fertiliser and oil is used as a tool of coercion. Transits through the strait have come to a near standstill. Unlawful Houthis attacks also threaten shipping through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, and as we have heard, The World Food Programme has estimated that the crisis and disruptions resulting from the Middle East conflict have pushed an additional 6.1 million people into acute food insecurity. And as we also have heard, World Food Programme warns that further 45 million people could be pushed into acute hunger, many of them far from any frontline. The situation heavily impacts humanitarian aid provision by spiking global fuel prices, inflating shipping and insurance costs, and delaying critical medical, food, and nutrition supplies. These disruptions worsen food insecurity in vulnerable regions worldwide. And the answer is clear. The Strait of Hormuz must be reopened immediately. The right of passage must be upheld. And this morning, our briefers have called for greater action from this Council. We join that call. We view Resolution 2417 as a powerful tool, but its potential remains untapped, particularly when it comes to early warning. The Security Council must play its part. Around this table, we should address patterns, not only individual emergencies. And early warning must spark early action. Secretary-General, that is why Denmark welcomes your initiative in establishing the Task Force on the Strait of Hormuz. The safe passage of fertilizers must be ensured, and we recognize your efforts in setting up this humanitarian mechanism. Denmark is also ready to contribute to the defensive and independent multinational military mission in the Strait of Hormuz, in support of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, when conditions allow. Excellencies, words matter here, especially from this Council. When infrastructure is destroyed, when farmers are attacked and their land is seized, When the UN and its humanitarian partners are blocked from doing their job, we must speak up. But speaking up is definitely not enough. Resolution 2417 reminds us of the tools we have in order to act, from early warning to restrictive measures to ensure accountability. What is needed is the will to use these tools. This work can be supported by new technologies. Satellite data with patterns of obstruction or attacks. Digital access to areas where physical access is denied. And in this way, denial of physical access can no longer mean denial of the truth. Finally, in emergencies, global food security supply chains must be protected. They are critical civilian infrastructure. They put food on tables thousands of miles away. Humanitarian cargo, fertilizers and energy products must be granted safe passage. Excellences, in closing, going forward, let us make the right choices in this Council and make use of the tools at our disposal. Support tangible measures to address the humanitarian impact on aid blockages. And whenever relevant, call out that the use of starvation as a method of warfare is clearly prohibited under international humanitarian law. Consider the use of sanction measures where appropriate. Utilize existing frameworks and new technology for early warning and support. The millions on the brink of famine around the world are looking to us to do exactly just that, and we cannot let them down. Thank you. And I now resume my function as President of the Council and will give the floor to Her Excellency Ms. Dace Belbane, Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs of Latvia, please.

Thank you, Mr. President, and let me thank the Danish Presidency for convening this meeting. I would like to thank Secretary General for his personal presence and his introduction to this significant topic. And thank you to Mr. Skou and Dr. Benoit for their powerful interventions of this morning. They have painted an irrefutable picture of a stark reality. Conflict continues to put food security at risk and civilians continue to pay the price. On the overall picture, while global hunger has declined, over 600 million people were affected by hunger in 2025. Behind this metric are families, women and children whose daily life is reduced to a single struggle, securing enough food to survive. In 2026, the risk of famine persists or has been identified in four countries or territories. Let me be clear, these famines are not natural disasters they are man made and they are entirely preventable. In Gaza acute food insecurity remains a daily reality for civilians compounded by repeated disruptions to supply chains and severe restrictions on humanitarian access. Given their low or non-existent income, the vast majority of families are largely dependent on the aid delivered by the UN and international NGOs. In Sudan, more than 20 million people face high levels of acute food insecurity. Yet the fighting between the Sudanese armed forces and the Rapid Support Forces continues. It displaces communities, destroys livelihoods and disrupts the very systems on which civilians depend. Markets have been repeatedly targeted by drones, while attacks on humanitarian and commercial convoys and critical trade routes continues to hinder access to food. The situation in hunger hotspots like Yemen, South Sudan, Haiti, Nigeria, Afghanistan and elsewhere requires our attention and swift action. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has also had far-reaching consequences globally, with severe disruptions to energy markets and a growing impact on global food security. This is a stark reminder that disruptions to critical trade routes can rapidly translate into consequences far beyond the immediate conflict zone. At the same time, climate change is intensifying food and water insecurity, especially for communities dependent on subsistence farming already affected by conflict and with limited capacity to withstand further shocks. Mr. President, there is a fundamental principle we must not lose sight of. Food must never be used as a weapon of war. The deliberate destruction of agricultural land and essential infrastructure necessary to sustain civilian life cannot be normalized as a feature of warfare. And this brings me to Russia's full scale aggression against Ukraine. Ukraine has long played a vital role in global food security. Before Russia's full scale war of aggression, Ukrainian food procured through the World Food Programme fed around 400 million people in humanitarian emergencies. Even under relentless attacks, Ukrainian farmers have continued to produce and supply food to crisis affected populations, including in Gaza, Sudan, Yemen and Nigeria. Yet Russia continues to target Ukrainian ports and grain harvests, humanitarian infrastructure and civilian merchant shipping, deliberately disrupting global food supplies. These are not only acts of aggression against Ukraine, but crimes against the world's most vulnerable, using food as a weapon. Latvia calls on the international community to take a strong diplomatic stance and demand an end to these attacks and restrictions. Russia must not be allowed to hold the hungry hostage. An immediate, full and unconditional ceasefire is essential to ending Russia's aggression and ensuring Ukraine's vital role in global food security. Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished members of the Council, the Democratic Republic of the Congo would like to thank Denmark for convening this open debate devoted to an issue that lies at the heart of international peace and security. The situation in many conflict zones, together with disruptions to global supply chains, demonstrates that food security is now inseparable from peace, stability and international security. The consequences of conflicts, go far beyond the areas of direct combat. Mr. President, in light of this reality, the Democratic Republic of the Congo believes that the Security Council must give resolution 2417 a fully operational scope by making prevention a genuine instrument of action. Early warning can only be meaningful if it leads to early, coordinated and proportioned action based on identified risks. In this regard, signals of worsening food insecurity, should be considered relevant elements in the analysis of situations that may threaten international peace and security. This approach must go hand in hand with stronger protection of critical infrastructure, markets and supply corridors, as well as the guarantee of safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access. Food and other goods indispensable for the survival of civilian populations must never be used as instruments of war or pressure. And this requires adequate and predictable financing, strengthening local production markets, improved storage and distribution capacities, and investment in agricultural technologies adapted to the effects of climate change. It is also essential to strengthen coordination amongst humanitarian action, development policies, conflict prevention efforts and peacekeeping operations. Such an approach will help avoid fragmented responses and better address the root causes of food insecurity. Mr. President, The experience of Africa, and particularly that of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, strongly reminds us of a fundamental reality. Hunger cannot be separated from security. In the DRC, millions of people face acute insecurity. Conflicts in North Kivu and South Kivu and Ituri have caused massive population displacement and disrupted agricultural production, supply chains, and access to humanitarian assistance. When a family abandons its land to flee violence, it loses not only its home, but also its ability to produce food, to sustain itself, and above all, to rebuild its future. And this is why urgent and sustainable responses must also aim to secure production areas, revive agriculture locally, modernise rural infrastructure and mobilise the investments needed to develop agricultural value chains. Mr. President, The Democratic Republic of the Congo reaffirms its commitment to an approach that places communities at the centre of prevention and response efforts, while strengthening national capacities in service delivery, agricultural production and resilience. The prevention of food crises must become an integral component of conflict prevention. Mr. President, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which itself experiences the human, social and economic consequences of conflict, knows that hunger cannot be regarded merely as a humanitarian tragedy. When hunger takes hold, persists and worsens, it weakens societies, it fuels displacement, it exacerbates tensions and can become a powerful driver of instability and conflict. Food security is therefore inseparable from peace, stability and development. The challenge before us, therefore, is clear. We must move from reaction to prevention, from emergency response to resilience, and from fragmentation to collective, coherent, and anticipatory action. The prevention of food insecurity must be fully integrated into efforts to prevent and resolve conflict. In conclusion, the Democratic Republic of the Congo reaffirms its determination to work with the Secretary-General, the Security Council, the United Nations system, Member States and regional partners to strengthen the resilience of food systems, to protect civilian populations and address the structural causes of vulnerability. This is our collective responsibility. It is to act before hunger turns into famine and before famine, in turn, becomes a driver of conflict and instability. Preventing hunger means preserving human dignity. Preventing hunger means strengthening resilience and, ultimately, preventing hunger also means preserving peace. I thank you.

Mr. President, I welcome your presiding, Mr. Lars Loker Rasmussen, Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Denmark, of this meeting, and I extend my thanks to His Excellency, Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary General of the United Nations, and Mr. Carl Skou, the Acting Director of the World Food Programme and Dr. Benoit from Action Against Hunger for their valuable briefings. Eight years since the adoption of resolution 2417 in 2018 on conflict-induced hunger, food security conditions continue to deteriorate amid the persistence of existing conflicts and the outbreak of new ones. As a co-focal point together with Denmark on the hunger and conflict file at the Security Council, the Kingdom of Bahrain looks forward to today's discussion contributing to strengthening the implementation of the resolution and supporting efforts to prevent conflict-related food insecurity. Madam President, I would like to focus on three points. First, the close link between hunger and conflict. The Kingdom of Bahrain affirms the importance of continuing to build on resolution 2417, which established the link between conflict and food insecurity and underscored the need to protect civilian objects, ensure humanitarian access and strengthen early warning. The latest United Nations report on hunger hotspots identified 13 countries and territories where food insecurity is expected to worsen, with conflict remaining the primary driver in 12 of them, with Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen and Palestine classified among the most severe cases. These findings underscore the importance of urgent action by the Security Council before these risks escalate into broader humanitarian crises. Second, given the long term impact of conflicts on food security, including damage to agricultural and arable land and infrastructure, the proliferation of unexploded ordinance and the displacement of farming communities. The resilience of food systems during and after conflicts takes on great importance. The Kingdom of Bahrain affirms that this requires supporting communities capacity to restore food production, protecting infrastructure and taking practical steps to ensure the continuity of supply chains. Third, As the nature of conflicts evolves and their impact broadens, including the increasing use of drones and the risks this poses to the delivery of assistance, the need emerges to strengthen the protection of humanitarian operations and ensure the delivery of food to civilians safely and without obstruction. The repercussions of conflict also extend to global supply chains. as clearly demonstrated by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which nearly 30% of global fertilizer trade passes, making any disruption in the region have a direct impact on fertilizer markets. global fertilizer markets. In this regard, the Kingdom of Bahrain affirms that protecting the freedom of navigation and the security of international waterways is not merely a security or trade matter, but is directly linked to global food security. When conflicts disrupt the flow of food, fertilizer, and energy to markets, their humanitarian effects extend to peoples who are not party to those conflicts. disproportionately burdening the most vulnerable states and communities. The Kingdom of Bahrain stresses the necessity for the Security Council to shoulder its responsibilities by taking firm and deterrent measures to compel Iran to immediately cease all hostile acts, respect freedom of navigation and ensure the security and safety of commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and other international waterways. and not to use the Strait as a tool of pressure or economic coercion, considering this essential to safeguarding energy security, ensuring stable food and medicine supplies, as well as guaranteeing the flow of global trade and consolidating security, stability and prosperity in the region and the world. Madam President, addressing the challenges related to food security, requires close and sustained coordination among member states, international and regional organizations, humanitarian actors and the private sector in a manner that enhances the continuity of agricultural production and supply chains, as well as the resilience of food systems while upholding international law and IHL. In closing, while conflicts continue, to cast their shadow over civilians and food security. The council has mechanisms available and at its disposal that can be used effectively and appropriately to prevent the escalation of humanitarian crises. Food security must not become an acceptable casualty of conflict. Rather, its protection must remain an essential part of effort aimed at protecting civilians and promoting peace and security. I thank you.

Thank you, Madam President. We thank Denmark for convening this important debate. And we also thank the Secretary General for his insightful remarks and recommendations that he offered today. The global environment today demonstrates a disturbing two-way dynamic. Conflicts, including situations of foreign occupation, are driving hunger on a massive scale, while hunger and economic desperation are, in turn, aggravating fragility and heightening the risk of conflict. The facts before us are sobering. The 2026 global report on food crisis found that 266 million people faced acute food insecurity last year. Acute hunger has doubled over the past decade. Today, 70% of acutely food insecure people live in fragile or conflict affected regions. latest FAO WFP assessment identifies 13 hunger hotspots with conflict and violence the primary driver in 12 of them. Resolution 2417 recognized this nexus eight years ago. The challenge before us today is not the absence of norms, but their effective implementation as emphasized by the SG the briefers and many council members. Madam President, it is a matter of grave concern that starvation and collective punishment continue to be used to advance military or political objectives in stark violation of international humanitarian law and Security Council resolutions. Nowhere has the failure to uphold these obligations been more stark than in Gaza. The deprivation of food and other essentials, restrictions on humanitarian assistance, and destruction of civilian infrastructure have inflicted unbearable suffering on the Palestinian people. Patterns of devastation are also evident in Yemen, Sudan, South Sudan, Haiti, and other protracted conflict situations, including foreign occupied territories. where livelihoods have collapsed and millions are now dependent on humanitarian assistance for survival. As the president, recent developments have demonstrated that food security consequences of conflict can extend far beyond the immediate theaters of hostilities. The conflict in Ukraine was a stark illustration. There must be safe, rapid, and unhindered humanitarian access. Humanitarian personnel must be able to operate freely, safely, and assistance must reach those in need without impediment. Accountability for deliberate obstruction or delays is a must. Third, early warning leads to early action. Credible assessments by the Secretary General, WFP, FAO, and other relevant UN entities should enable timely attention and preventive engagement. In fact, limited water resources is an impediment to food production and to resilience. And that is why Egypt reiterates the importance of the link between water security and food security. Funding and technology. And capacity building needs to be available, and investment needs to be made for the good management and use of water for agriculture and food production. To conclude, I would like to reaffirm the importance of institutional role. The Security Council has a principal role to play, namely, maintain international peace and security. And the specialized agency of the United Nations, and international financial institutions and other organizations have economic, specific economic roles in coordination and was respecting each other's mandates and specialization. I thank you.
Representative of Egypt for the statement. And I now give the floor to the representative of India.

Madam President, India thanks Denmark for convening this important open debate. We also thank the Secretary General and the other briefers for their valuable insights. Food insecurity remains one of the gravest humanitarian consequences of armed conflict. Today's conflicts increasingly generate ripple effects far beyond the immediate theater of hostilities. Disruptions to energy markets, fertilizer supplies, maritime transport, humanitarian logistics and agricultural trade have demonstrated how regional conflicts can threaten food security across the world. with the greatest burden falling on developing countries that are highly import dependent. Let us nevertheless remain clear about the causality of this challenge. Food insecurity is fundamentally a consequence of conflict, political instability, and underdevelopment, not their root cause. While the Security Council has an important role in responding to threats to international peace and security, building resilient, food secure societies remains primarily the responsibility of national governments, supported by the UN development system and the Rome-based agencies. Resolution 2417 of the Security Council on conflict-induced food insecurity provides an important framework by recognizing the relationship between armed conflict and hunger. Early warning should therefore not be limited to identifying deteriorating humanitarian conditions on the ground. It should also include timely assessments of disruptions to critical supply chains, including food, fertilizer, fuel, and humanitarian logistics, drawing upon the technical expertise of the Food and Agricultural Organization, the World Food Program, and other relevant agencies. Such assessments must remain objective, evidence-based, and free from politicization. Madam President, the Council's immediate priority should be to mitigate the humanitarian consequences of conflict. This requires facilitating safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access, supporting deconfliction arrangements where appropriate, and ensuring that the Council's own measures, including sanctions regimes, do not inadvertently impede humanitarian assistance or legitimate food and agricultural trade. Equally important is the protection of civilian infrastructure essential for food security, including agricultural land, irrigation systems, storage facilities, transport corridors and ports. Equally important is the need to preserve the safety and freedom of navigation for commercial shipping in accordance with international law. Secure and predictable maritime trade routes are indispensable for the uninterrupted movement of food, fertilizers, fuel, and other essential commodities. Disruptions to commercial shipping during conflicts can have cascading effects far beyond the immediate region, disproportionately affecting food importing developing countries and humanitarian operations. The international community must therefore work collectively to safeguard critical sea lanes and maritime infrastructure while ensuring that legitimate commercial trade and humanitarian shipments are able to proceed without undue impediment. At the same time, lasting resilience cannot be delivered through humanitarian action alone. Member states, international financial institutions, Regional organizations and development partners must work together to strengthen domestic agricultural production, diversify supply chains, improve storage and logistics infrastructure, and promote climate resilient agriculture. Predictable and affordable access to fertilizers, quality seeds, technology and concessional finance remains indispensable, particularly for developing countries. Open, transparent, and rules-based trade in food and agricultural inputs also remains critical to global food security. India's own experience underscores the centrality of sustained nationally owned investments in resilient food systems. The National Food Security Act provides a statutory entitlement to subsidize food grain, direct benefit transfers to over 110 million farming households under the PM Kisan, which have strengthened the economic resilience of small and marginal producers. India's championing of the International Year of Millets in 2023 has catalyzed global attention to climate resilient, nutrient rich crops as a viable pathway to diversified food security. These efforts underpinned by digital public infrastructure and climate adaptive agricultural practices have enabled India to remain both food secure and a net contribution to global food supply. We remain committed to sharing these experiences through South-South cooperation and development partnerships. Furthermore, ocean atmospheric variability, such as El Nino, add an additional layer of vulnerability. They disrupt monsoon patterns, reduce crop yields, and strain water resources, compounding the food security problems. Addressing this requires strengthened international cooperation, and we look forward to working with the international community in that regard. Madam President, The Secretary-General's good offices can play a valuable role in facilitating dialogue, reducing tensions, and supporting humanitarian access where appropriate. The broader UN system should continue to leverage scientific expertise, operational capabilities, and timely data to inform decision-making. Such efforts should complement, not substitute for national ownership and nationally-led responses. India firmly believes that peace, development, and food security are mutually reinforcing. The Security Council should focus on fulfilling its mandate by addressing conflict, facilitating humanitarian access, and supporting conditions for peace. The General Assembly, the ECOSOC, the UN Development System, and the Rome-based agencies should continue to lead the long-term response to food insecurity. Finally, Over reliance on any single model of production would be counterproductive as they are vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions, economic coercion, and weaponization. We must encourage small and marginal farmers to enhance their productivity and contribute to ensuring food security in developing countries of the global south. We must also encourage climate resilient crops such as millets rather than limit conceptions of food security to the biggest staple grain crops such as rice, wheat, and corn. By acting within their respective mandates and in a spirit of genuine multilateral cooperation, the United Nations system can better prevent food crises. I thank you, Madam President.
I thank the representative of India for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of Switzerland.

Madam President, Switzerland thanks Denmark for convening this open debate. Eight years after its adoption, resolution 2417, remains as relevant as ever. Armed conflict continues to be one of the primary drivers of food insecurity. In 2025, for the first time this century, famine was declared simultaneously in two separate contexts, parts of the Gaza Strip and Sudan. In 2026, the risk of famine persists in both contexts. Across armed conflicts, violations of international humanitarian law have exacerbated food insecurity. These include attacks affecting civilian objects and infrastructure essential to the survival of the civilian population, restrictions on humanitarian access, and other impediments to the delivery of essential goods. Russia's war against Ukraine and the conflicts in the Middle East, demonstrate that armed conflicts and repeated and related violations of international law can have major consequences for global food security. Disruptions to maritime routes have exposed the fragility of global supply chains. Conflicts undermine food systems by disrupting agricultural production, markets, trade routes, energy supplies and access to fuel and fertilizers. These developments underscore the importance of investing in resilient and sustainable food systems and reducing external dependencies. They also reinforce the urgent need to translate the commitments contained in resolution 2417 into concrete action. Switzerland calls on the Council to strengthen its implementation in three priority areas, First, we must strengthen prevention by making better use of early warning information and acting before crises reach catastrophic levels. Bridging the gap between warning and action requires political will and the council's timely engagement. Secondly, we must preserve humanitarian space and ensure respect for international humanitarian law. This includes protecting civilians and objects indispensable to their survival, and ensuring safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. In this regard, we also recall resolution 2573 on the protection of civilian infrastructure and resolution 2730 on the protection of humanitarian and UN personnel. Thirdly, We must combat impunity by ensuring that violations of international humanitarian law are investigated and those responsible held to account. The use of starvation of civilians as a method of warfare is prohibited under international humanitarian law and constitutes a war crime. Harm to food security, whether caused by disruptions to shipping routes or by other conflict-related factors, must never be accepted as an inevitable collateral consequence of armed conflict. Madam President, addressing conflict-induced hunger must remain a priority for this Council. Financial support and greater resilience are necessary, but they cannot on their own address the root causes of conflict-related food insecurity. prevention, mediation, dialogue and the peaceful resolution of conflicts are indispensable. Switzerland remains committed to these efforts, including in its capacity as a host state and a facilitator of mediation processes. I thank you.
Thank you, Switzerland, for the statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of New Zealand.

President, I thank all those involved in responding to this devastating issue. Conflict remains one of the greatest drivers of global food insecurity. Through the destruction of farms and fisheries, the displacement of communities, restrictions on humanitarian access, and the disruption of trade and supply chains, armed conflict undermines access to sufficient, safe, and affordable food. Civilians invariably bear the heaviest burden. New Zealand remains deeply concerned by the devastating humanitarian situations in Gaza and Sudan. Access to food, water, and essential services has been severely affected, while humanitarian agencies continue to face significant challenges in reaching those in need. International humanitarian law is clear. Access to food and other goods essential for survival must never be denied, and humanitarian assistance must be able to reach those in need safely, rapidly, and without obstruction. But the impacts of conflict are not confined to conflict zones. Recent events have demonstrated how disruptions to agricultural production, trade routes, energy supplies, and global markets have far-reaching consequences for food security around the world. Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine demonstrated how conflict can reverberate through global food systems. Disruptions to grain exports, fertilizer supplies, and energy markets contributed to higher food prices and increased food insecurity far beyond Europe. Disruptions to maritime shipping routes, including through the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, have reinforced the continued vulnerability of global food systems to geopolitical instability. For Pacific Island countries at the end of some of the world's longest and most vulnerable supply chains, these are not abstract geopolitical concerns. Food security is increasingly linked to events far beyond our region. For countries already facing climate-related pressures, conflict-driven shocks to food and energy markets have direct consequences for food affordability, livelihoods, and economic resilience. The ramifications of conflicts on the other side of the world remind us how the three pillars of the UN are deeply interconnected. President, the Security Council has already recognized the connection between armed conflict and hunger through resolution 2417. Eight years after its adoption, our focus must be on translating that framework into earlier and more effective action. We need to make better use of early warning. The Council should receive timely and systematic information when conflict threatens serious food insecurity. including where effects extend beyond the immediate conflict zone through disruptions to energy and fertilizer supplies, humanitarian operations, or critical land and maritime trade routes. We should also make greater use of the Secretary General's good offices and the expertise of the wider UN system. Finally, where conflict threatens critical food supply routes or obstructs humanitarian access, the Council should support diplomatic efforts to maintain those routes and enable food and agricultural products to reach those who depend upon them. International law guarantees freedom of navigation and transit passage under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and customary international law. Upholding these fundamental rights in peacetime and conflict is critical for maritime trade and protecting global food security. This Council should address the drivers of conflict, support humanitarian access, and uphold the international rules and institutions that underpin food security for millions. Through our international development cooperation programme, New Zealand supports climate resilient agriculture and food systems to sustain livelihoods. New Zealand also funds the World Food Programme to alleviate hunger amongst the world's most vulnerable populations, including those affected directly by conflict. These investments help communities withstand the combined impacts of climate change, economic shocks, and disruptions to global food and agricultural supply chains. President, I conclude by affirming that not only should hunger never be used as a tool of war, it should not be seen as an inevitable consequence of conflict either. Thank you.

Thank you Madam President. Let me begin by thanking Denmark for convening this important open debate. I also thank the Secretary General, Mr. Cosgrove, the WFP acting executive director and Dr. Perin Benoit, the co-CEO of Action Against Hunger for their briefings. Excellencies, eight years after the adoption of the Security Council Resolution 2417, the intrinsic link between armed conflict and food insecurity remains stark. Food insecurity remains at alarmingly high level with conflict continuing to be one of its principal drivers. The weaponization of hunger, destruction of objects indispensable to civilian survival, disruptions of global supply chains, and blockage of maritime trade routes have pushed millions of civilians into increasingly vulnerable conditions. Developing countries across the global south often bear the brunt of these conflicts far beyond their borders. Against this backdrop, Indonesia wishes to emphasize three key points. First, we must stand firm to ensure that starvation is never tolerated as a weapon of war. Such action represents a grave violation of international humanitarian law and constitutes a war crime. In this context, Indonesia draws this Council's attention to the alarming findings of the UN Special Committee to Investigate Israeli Practices, which documents serious breaches of international humanitarian and human rights law in Gaza, revealing a catastrophe where hunger is systematically weaponized. When a UN mandated body warns of such systematic starvation, the Council must act to ensure unhindered humanitarian access and ensure that such action will not go without consequences. Second, the Council must ensure accountability for those who weaponize hunger. In line with resolution 2417, the Council must use its authority consistently against any party that deliberately blocks humanitarian aid and destroys food infrastructure. Reports from the Secretary-General and other UN entities Documenting these violations should serve as a strong basis to ensure that accountability is upheld. Impunity does not only embolden perpetrators, it further erodes the credibility of the Council itself. The Council must therefore close this accountability gap to uphold the integrity of international humanitarian law and prevent starvation from becoming a normal feature of today's conflict. Third, we must protect global food and agricultural supply chains from the crossfire of geopolitical conflicts. Disruptions to energy flows, maritime trade routes, and fertilizer supplies have severely trained global food production and inflated price worldwide. Food security must never become a casualty of war or collateral damage of conflicts. We urge all member states and regional organizations to support efforts to protect vital arteries of global trade. In this regard, we welcome the Secretary-General's good offices and recent UN initiatives, including the Task Force on the Strait of Hormuz, to ensure safe, orderly and reliable transit for humanitarian and essential commodities. Madam President, starvation in conflict is preventable. To this end, this Council must show that international law still carries weight by confronting those who starve civilians as a tactic of war. Let us turn our resolution into decisive action before conflict starves the future of yet another generation.

I thank the representative of Indonesia for the statement. There are still a number of speakers remaining on my list for this meeting. I intend, with the concurrence of members of the Council, to suspend the meeting until 3:00 PM. This meeting is suspended.
